title: Anthony Beaman (Chief Running Bull)
summary: Anthony Beaman (1879–1963), also documented as Chief Running Bull and Anthony “Did” Beaman, was a Shinnecock medicine man and cultural participant whose story connects family history, botanical knowledge, and public pageant records.
content:
Anthony Beaman (July 7, 1879–November 22, 1963), also documented as Chief Running Bull and Anthony “Did” Beaman, was a Shinnecock medicine man and cultural participant. Family records, ethnographic collections, and Shinnecock pageant histories preserve parts of his life across the early and mid-twentieth century. A circa-1934 photograph caption identifies “Anthony Beaman-Chief Running Bull” and describes him as a tribal medicine man. The caption supports the recorded name, but it does not establish that “Chief” was a Shinnecock governmental office.1

Family connections

A photograph caption in The History and Archaeology of the Montauk possibly dates the wedding of Eliza Fowler Beaman and Anthony Beaman to 1905. It identifies Eliza with her father, George Lewis Fowler Sr., and her husband Anthony, who is described as Shinnecock. Because the caption qualifies the date and does not identify the ceremony location, this biography preserves that uncertainty rather than assigning a precise wedding place.2

Stories, plants, and historical medicine

Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians records that Anthony and Eliza Beaman supplied five tales and that both contributed herbal material. The same volume attributes additional plant knowledge to them. A later historical narrative prepared during the Shinnecock federal-acknowledgment process reports that community informants remembered Anthony “Did” Beaman and Seymour Eleazer as medicine men who practiced into the 1940s. These records document community knowledge and historical practice; they are not presented as medical instructions.3

Pageants and public memory

A chronology of Shinnecock ceremonies names Running Bull, Anthony Beaman, the Medicine Man, among the people present at the 1914 Shinnecock pageant on the reservation. A separate caption identifies him in a circa-1934 group photograph at Conscience Point in North Sea. Together, these records show how named Shinnecock participants carried community knowledge into public historical presentations while remaining more than the roles assigned to them in pageant programs.4

Reading the surviving record

Much of the surviving public record appears in captions, family compilations, ethnographic collections, and later historical narratives. Those sources preserve Anthony Beaman’s names and roles, but they do not provide a complete life history. This biography therefore keeps locations broad, does not infer a residence or ceremonial route, and distinguishes documented captions from claims about political office.

References

  • Shinnecock Indian Nation, Ancestors from 19th and 20th century, p. 2.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History, vol. VI (1983), pp. 345 and 351.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The History and Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), p. 376.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, vol. IV (1980), pp. 115 and 119–121.
  • Jack Campisi / Research Associates, Draft Copy of Historical Narrative of Shinnecock—Petition for Acknowledgment (first draft Nov. 25, 1994), p. 27.
why_this_matters: Anthony Beaman’s surviving record keeps a named Shinnecock knowledge keeper visible across family history, plant lore, and twentieth-century public memory while showing the care needed when captions and later compilations provide only part of a life.
activity_update_summary: Added a source-supported biography of Anthony Beaman (Chief Running Bull) with family history, documented knowledge, pageant records, and three linked Historic Moments.
